title: The God of All Comfort
subtitle: 2 Corinthians 1:1–11
description: A strained relationship, a painful visit behind them, and a letter that opens with the God of all comfort before any explanation.
paragraphs: Paul writes to Corinth again, this time from Macedonia, on the road that will bring him to them for a third visit. The relationship behind the letter is strained. A visit between the two letters went badly, and after it went a letter Paul wrote through tears. What came back with Titus, who carried word between them, was good enough that this letter can be written at all. But it does not open with the trouble. It opens with comfort.

The greeting runs: “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother,” writing “To the church of God in Corinth, together with all the saints throughout Achaia:” Then the familiar words, carrying their usual weight: “Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

Then Paul blesses God before he explains anything. “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of compassion and the God of all comfort.” The reason sits inside the blessing. God is the one “who comforts us in all our troubles,” and the comfort is not meant to stop with the people who receive it. It comes “so that we can comfort those in any trouble with the comfort we ourselves have received from God.”

The sharing runs in both directions. “For just as the sufferings of Christ overflow to us, so also through Christ our comfort overflows.” “If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation”; if they are comforted, “it is for your comfort” too, and Paul says that comfort works something in them: it “accomplishes in you patient endurance of the same sufferings we experience.” And his hope for the Corinthians stands on that sharing: it is sure, “because we know that just as you share in our sufferings, so also you will share in our comfort.”

Then the letter says why comfort is not a theory for the man writing it. “We do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of the hardships we encountered in the province of Asia.” What the hardship in Asia was, the letter never describes. Paul says what it did. “We were under a burden far beyond our ability to endure, so that we despaired even of life.”

The despair had a direction, and Paul reads it backward as a lesson. “Indeed, we felt we were under the sentence of death, in order that we would not trust in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead.” What Asia taught the apostle was not to lean harder on himself. It taught him where to lean.

The rescue is as plain as the peril. “He has delivered us from such a deadly peril, and He will deliver us. In Him we have placed our hope that He will yet again deliver us,” and the Corinthians stand inside that hope rather than outside it. The deliverance comes “as you help us by your prayers,” so that “many will give thanks on our behalf for the favor shown us in answer to their prayers.” The first thing this difficult letter asks of a difficult church is not an apology. It is thanks for prayers they already prayed.

title: To Spare You I Stayed Away
subtitle: 2 Corinthians 1:12–24
description: The changed travel plan defended: a clear conscience, a Christ who is never yes and no, and a visit postponed to spare them.
paragraphs: Comfort given, Paul turns to the charge hanging over the whole letter: that he cannot be trusted to keep his word. He had planned a visit, announced it, and not come. Before he explains the change, he states the ground he stands on. “For this is our boast: Our conscience testifies that we have conducted ourselves in the world, and especially in relation to you,” in a holiness and sincerity that are from God. The sentence finishes his way, in two pieces, and both pieces matter: “in the holiness and sincerity that are from God” and “not in worldly wisdom, but in the grace of God.”

His letters, he insists, mean what they say. “For we do not write you anything that is beyond your ability to read and understand.” His hope is that the understanding will complete itself, “as you have already understood us in part,” until each side can boast of the other “in the day of our Lord Jesus.”

Then the plan itself. “Confident of this, I planned to visit you first, so that you might receive a double blessing.” The route was drawn: “I wanted to visit you on my way to Macedonia, and to return to you from Macedonia, and then to have you help me on my way to Judea.” Corinth twice, on the way out and on the way back. The visit did not happen, and the failure to appear became the evidence against him: a man whose yes means nothing.

Paul meets the charge with a question. “When I planned this, did I do it carelessly? Or do I make my plans by human standards,” ready to say yes and no in the same breath? His answer rises from his own conduct to God's. “But as surely as God is faithful, our message to you is not” a yes that is also a no. The Christ preached at Corinth was no such mixture: “For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was proclaimed among you by me and Silvanus and Timothy” was not yes and no, “but in Him it has always been” yes. Every promise of God finds that same yes in Christ: “For all the promises of God are” yes “in Christ. And so through Him, our” Amen “is spoken to the glory of God.”

The ground under both parties is God's own work. “Now it is God who establishes both us and you in Christ. He anointed us,” Paul writes, and he “placed His seal on us, and put His Spirit in our hearts as a pledge of what is to come.”

Then, at the end of the defense, the reason itself, sworn to. “I call God as my witness that it was in order to spare you that I did not return to Corinth.” The changed plan was not drift or deceit. A visit at that moment would have come as a reckoning, and Paul chose the letter instead of the confrontation. And lest the sparing sound like rule from a distance, he adds: “Not that we lord it over your faith, but we are fellow workers with you for your joy, because it is by faith that you stand firm.”

title: Forgive and Comfort Him
subtitle: 2 Corinthians 2:1–11
description: The punishment is sufficient: the church that disciplined the offender is now told to forgive him before sorrow swallows him.
paragraphs: Behind this letter stand two things the letter itself is our only record of. One is a visit Paul calls painful, which Acts never narrates. The other is a letter he wrote through tears, whose words we do not have. Both enter the story only in Paul's own references to them, and both are left exactly there.

The visit he would not repeat: “So I made up my mind not to make another painful visit to you.” His reason runs in a circle of shared joy and shared grief. “For if I grieve you, who is left to cheer me but those whom I have grieved?” So the confrontation went into writing instead of a room. “I wrote as I did so that on my arrival I would not be grieved by those who ought to make me rejoice. I had confidence in all of you, that you would share my joy.”

The letter behind those words was not written cold. “For through many tears I wrote you out of great distress and anguish of heart, not to grieve you but to let you know how much I love you.” Whether that letter is the one we call 1 Corinthians, the texts do not say plainly, and the telling does not decide it for them. What this letter reports is what the hard letter was for, and what it found when it arrived.

At the center of the trouble stood one man. Paul never names him, and he never says exactly what the man did. Whether he is the man of the earlier letter's fifth chapter, neither letter says, and this telling does not merge them. What this letter says is narrower and plainer. “Now if anyone has caused grief, he has not grieved me but all of you,” and then, split by Paul's own pause, “to some degree, not to overstate it.” The church acted. “The punishment imposed on him by the majority is sufficient for him.”

Sufficient is the word the whole episode turns on. The punishment has done its work, and Paul now argues in the opposite direction from the one a wounded apostle might be expected to take. “So instead, you ought to forgive and comfort him, so that he will not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.” Then, as a command wrapped in an appeal: “Therefore I urge you to reaffirm your love for him.”

The letter they are answering had been a test, and Paul says so. “My purpose in writing you was to see if you would stand the test and be obedient in everything.” They stood it in the discipline. The forgiving is the same obedience continued. “If you forgive anyone, I also forgive him. And if I have forgiven anything, I have forgiven it in the presence of Christ for your sake,” and the reason he gives reaches past the man to the enemy watching the church's mercy fail: “in order that Satan should not outwit us. For we are not unaware of his schemes.”

title: No Peace Without Titus
subtitle: 2 Corinthians 2:12–17
description: An open door at Troas left standing open, a procession of captives, and one fragrance received as life or as death.
paragraphs: The defense pauses, and Paul tells the Corinthians what the waiting cost him. After the letter of tears went to Corinth, he traveled north to Troas, the port city across the Aegean, and the work there was promising from the first day. “Now when I went to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ and a door stood open for me in the Lord,” the door was not the problem.

The problem was who was not there. Titus had been sent to Corinth, and Titus was the man who would carry the church's answer back. “I had no peace in my spirit, because I did not find my brother Titus there. So I said goodbye to them and went on to Macedonia.” An open door for the gospel, left standing open, because the apostle could not rest until he knew what his hard letter had done to people he loved. He crossed into Macedonia to meet the returning messenger sooner.

Then, mid-sentence almost, the letter breaks into thanks. “But thanks be to God, who always leads us triumphantly as captives in Christ and through us spreads everywhere the fragrance of the knowledge of Him.” The picture is a Roman victory procession, with Paul in the place of a captive being led, and the strange glory of it is that the captives carry the smell of the triumph with them. What they spread is knowledge of God, and it arrives the way a fragrance does, to everyone in range.

The fragrance does not land the same way on everyone. “For we are to God the sweet aroma of Christ among those who are being saved and those who are perishing.” Then the two receptions, stated flatly: “To the one we are an odor that brings death, to the other a fragrance that brings life.” The same scent, the same Christ, and the difference lies in the ones breathing it in. Paul lets the weight of that stand in a question he does not answer: “And who is qualified for such a task?”

His own claim is the plain one he keeps returning to. “For we are not like so many others, who peddle the word of God for profit. On the contrary, in Christ we speak before God with sincerity, as men sent from God.” The letter resumes its defense from there, but the detour has shown the reader the man writing it: restless without news of Corinth, and ready to walk away from an open door to go and get it.

title: Written on Human Hearts
subtitle: 2 Corinthians 3:1–18
description: No letters of recommendation: the church itself is the letter, and the new covenant outshines the glory on Moses' veiled face.
paragraphs: Traveling teachers in Paul's world carried letters of recommendation, credentials from people who could vouch for them. Paul opens this part of the letter by refusing the whole arrangement, half laughing at it. “Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Or do we need, like some people, letters of recommendation to you or from you?” His answer is the church itself. “You yourselves are our letter, inscribed on our hearts, known and read by everyone.”

Then he corrects even that. The letter is not really his handwriting at all. “It is clear that you are a letter from Christ, the result of our ministry, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.” The Corinthians' changed lives are the credential, written by a better hand than his, on living material instead of rock.

That is the ground of his confidence, and he locates it carefully. “Such confidence before God is ours through Christ.” Then the disclaimer that the whole letter keeps making: “Not that we are competent in ourselves to claim that anything comes from us, but our competence comes from God.” And the calling itself gets named: “And He has qualified us as ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.”

From there Paul measures the new ministry against the old one, and the comparison is an argument from lesser to greater. The ministry that came through Moses was glorious on its own terms: “if the ministry of death, which was engraved in letters on stone, came with such glory that the Israelites could not gaze at the face of Moses because of its fleeting glory,” then “will not the ministry of the Spirit be even more glorious?” If the ministry of condemnation carried glory, “how much more glorious is the ministry of righteousness!” The old glory is not denied. It is outshone: “Indeed, what was once glorious has no glory now in comparison to the glory that surpasses it.” And the old was fading while the new endures: “For if what was fading away came with glory, how much greater is the glory of that which endures!”

The difference shows in how the two ministries handle faces. “Therefore, since we have such a hope, we are very bold. We are not like Moses, who would put a veil over his face to keep the Israelites from gazing at the end of what was fading away.” But the veil outlasted Moses. “But their minds were closed. For to this day the same veil remains at the reading of the old covenant. It has not been lifted, because only in Christ can it be removed.” Whenever the old books are read, Paul says, “a veil covers their hearts,” and the removal has one condition and one promise: “But whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away.”

His last word on it is freedom. “Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. And we, who with unveiled faces all reflect the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into His image with intensifying glory, which comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit.” No veil, no fading, and faces that change by looking.

title: Treasure in Jars of Clay
subtitle: 2 Corinthians 4:1–18
description: Treasure in crackable containers, four blows with four survivals, and eyes fixed on what is unseen and eternal.
paragraphs: The ministry described in the last episode is the one Paul says he holds by mercy, and its first effect is endurance. “Therefore, since God in His mercy has given us this ministry, we do not lose heart.” The methods match the message: “we have renounced secret and shameful ways. We do not practice deceit, nor do we distort the word of God. On the contrary, by open proclamation of the truth, we commend ourselves to every man’s conscience in the sight of God.”

If the gospel still lands veiled on some hearers, Paul says the veil is not in the preaching. “And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so they cannot see the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.” What the apostles proclaim is never themselves: “For we do not proclaim ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.”

The light that unbelief cannot see is the same light that made the world. The God who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” has “made His light shine in our hearts to give us the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.” And that treasure rides in the plainest container available. “Now we have this treasure in jars of clay to show that this surpassingly great power is from God and not from us.” Clay pots, common and crackable, so that nobody mistakes the vessel for the source.

Then the catalogue of the cracking, four blows and four survivals. “We are hard pressed on all sides, but not crushed; perplexed, but not in despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed.” The pattern under the pressure is Christ's own: “We always carry around in our body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our body.” And the exchange runs toward the churches, as it did with comfort: “So then, death is at work in us, but life is at work in you.”

Why keep speaking under those terms? The psalm line Paul quotes stands at the head of his answer, and he takes it as his own confession: “I believed, therefore I have spoken.” The faith that speaks is a faith that knows the end: “knowing that the One who raised the Lord Jesus will also raise us with Jesus and present us with you in His presence.” All of it is outward bound: “All this is for your benefit, so that the grace that is extending to more and more people may cause thanksgiving to overflow, to the glory of God.”

So the chapter closes where it opened, on not losing heart, now with the arithmetic shown. “Though our outer self is wasting away, yet our inner self is being renewed day by day. For our light and momentary affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory that is far beyond comparison.” The eyes that measure it are fixed accordingly: “So we fix our eyes not on what is seen, but on what is unseen. For what is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal.”

title: Longing to Be Clothed
subtitle: 2 Corinthians 5:1–10
description: A tent and a building, a groaning that wants more covering rather than less, and the judgment seat named without softening.
paragraphs: The jars of clay from the last episode become a tent in this one, a dwelling meant to be taken down. Paul states the exchange as knowledge, not hopefulness. “For we know that if the earthly tent we live in is dismantled, we have a building from God, an eternal house in heaven, not built by human hands.” A tent comes down. A building stands. And the second dwelling is already spoken of as possessed, not merely promised: we have it.

Life in the tent is marked by groaning, and Paul is exact about what the groaning wants. “For in this tent we groan, longing to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling, because when we are clothed, we will not be found naked.” The wish is not to escape the body but to be covered by a better one. “For while we are in this tent, we groan under our burdens, because we do not wish to be unclothed but clothed, so that our mortality may be swallowed up by life.” Swallowed up is the direction: not mortality escaping life, but life consuming mortality.

The preparation and the guarantee are both God's. “And it is God who has prepared us for this very purpose and has given us the Spirit as a pledge of what is to come.” A pledge is a down payment in hand, part of the full amount already paid over, and Paul treats the Spirit in the heart that way here, as he did when the seal was named earlier in the letter.

Confidence follows from it, with the present arrangement stated honestly. “Therefore we are always confident, although we know that while we are at home in the body, we are away from the Lord. For we walk by faith, not by sight.” The preference is admitted out loud: “We are confident, then, and would prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord.” And the preference settles into a single ambition that covers either address: “So we aspire to please Him, whether we are at home in this body or away from it.”

Then the passage ends on the reason the ambition is serious, and Paul does not soften it. “For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, that each one may receive his due for the things done in the body, whether good or bad.” All of us, each one, the things done in the body. The man who has just written about being swallowed up by life writes this sentence in the same breath, and the telling leaves the two standing together exactly as he left them.

title: Be Reconciled to God
subtitle: 2 Corinthians 5:11–21
description: Christ's love compels: a new creation, a ministry of reconciliation, and the great exchange stated in a single sentence.
paragraphs: The judgment seat of the last episode is the engine of this one. “Therefore, since we know what it means to fear the Lord, we try to persuade men. What we are is clear to God, and I hope it is clear to your conscience as well.” Paul is not, he says again, commending himself. He is arming the Corinthians instead: “we are giving you an occasion to be proud of us, so that you can answer those who take pride in appearances rather than in the heart.” His own strangeness he leaves with God: “If we are out of our mind, it is for God; if we are of sound mind, it is for you.”

Underneath the persuasion sits the conviction that drives it. “For Christ’s love compels us, because we are convinced that One died for all, therefore all died. And He died for all, that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for Him who died for them and was raised again.” One death, counted for all; a life after it that no longer belongs to the one living it. That conviction retires the old way of sizing people up entirely: “So from now on we regard no one according to the flesh. Although we once regarded Christ in this way, we do so no longer.”

Then the sentence the whole passage is remembered by. “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away. Behold, the new has come!” Paul immediately traces it to its source: “All this is from God, who reconciled us to Himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation.”

The ministry gets defined in one long breath. God “was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ, not counting men’s trespasses against them. And He has committed to us the message of reconciliation.” So the apostles speak as envoys of the King who made the peace: “Therefore we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were making His appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ: Be reconciled to God.” The appeal lands in the middle of a letter to people already in the church, and Paul lets it land there, on them, before it goes anywhere else.

Last comes the exchange underneath everything, stated in one sentence with nothing added to cushion it. “God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.” The sinless one made sin; the reconciled made righteous. That is where the episode stops, because that is where Paul stops, with the whole ministry hanging on that single trade.

title: Now Is the Day of Salvation
subtitle: 2 Corinthians 6:1–13
description: Grace that can be received in vain, a catalogue of endurance and paradox, and a father's plea for open hearts in fair exchange.
paragraphs: The appeal to be reconciled turns urgent. “As God’s fellow workers, then, we urge you not to receive God’s grace in vain.” Behind the urgency stands a quoted promise about timing. God says: “In the time of favor I heard you, and in the day of salvation I helped you.” Paul's comment on the quotation is two short sentences, and they do the pressing: “Behold, now is the time of favor; now is the day of salvation!” The day the prophecy pointed at is not coming. It is today, and grace can be received in a way that wastes it.

Then Paul lays out the conduct that guards the message. “We put no obstacle in anyone’s way, so that no one can discredit our ministry. Rather, as servants of God we commend ourselves in every way.” What follows is the commendation, and it is not a résumé of achievements. It falls in three bands. First, the conditions endured: “in great endurance; in troubles, hardships, and calamities; in beatings, imprisonments, and riots; in labor, sleepless nights, and hunger.”

Second, the character carried through the conditions: “in purity, knowledge, patience, and kindness; in the Holy Spirit and in sincere love; in truthful speech and in the power of God; with the weapons of righteousness in the right hand and in the left.” Third, the verdicts of the world, each one answered by its opposite: “through glory and dishonor, slander and praise; viewed as imposters, yet genuine; unknown, yet well-known; dying, and yet we live on; punished, yet not killed; sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; poor, yet making many rich; having nothing, and yet possessing everything.”

The catalogue done, the letter's voice drops from apostle to father. “We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians. Our hearts are open wide.” If there is a narrowness in this relationship, he says, it is not on his side: “It is not our affection, but yours, that is restrained.” And the request that ends the episode is a fair trade between a father and his children, feeling for feeling: “open wide your hearts also.”

title: God Comforted the Downcast
subtitle: 2 Corinthians 6:14–7:16
description: The call to separation, promises stacked from the older books, and Titus's arrival in Macedonia with the church's answer.
paragraphs: Here the letter turns to the company the Corinthians keep, and the call is separation, argued as a run of questions with only one possible answer. “Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership can righteousness have with wickedness? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness? What harmony is there between Christ and Belial? Or what does a believer have in common with an unbeliever? What agreement can exist between the temple of God and idols?”

The ground of the call is who the church already is. “For we are the temple of the living God. As God has said:” and then the promises are stacked one on another, God's own words from the older books. “I will dwell with them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be My people.” “Therefore come out from among them and be separate, says the Lord. Touch no unclean thing, and I will receive you.” “I will be a Father to you, and you will be My sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty.”

Promises like that ask something back. “Therefore, beloved, since we have these promises, let us cleanse ourselves from everything that defiles body and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.” And at once the letter is personal again: “Make room for us in your hearts. We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have exploited no one.” No condemnation is intended. “I have said before that you so occupy our hearts that we live and die together with you.”

Then Paul tells them, at last, what happened in Macedonia, and the letter's whole journey comes into view. “For when we arrived in Macedonia, our bodies had no rest, but we were pressed from every direction,” and the pressure is named inside and out: “conflicts on the outside, fears within.” This is the man who left an open door at Troas standing open because Titus was not there. “But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the arrival of Titus, and not only by his arrival, but also by the comfort he had received from you. He told us about your longing, your mourning, and your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced all the more.”

The news let Paul say the hard thing about his own hard letter. “Even if I caused you sorrow by my letter, I do not regret it. Although I did regret it,” because “I see that my letter caused you sorrow, but only for a short time,” he rejoices now, “not because you were made sorrowful, but because your sorrow led you to repentance.” The distinction underneath the relief is stated as a rule: “Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret, but worldly sorrow brings death.” And Corinth's sorrow had been the godly kind, with fruit to show: “what earnestness, what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what alarm, what longing, what zeal, what vindication!”

The letter he wrote, he explains, was never mainly about the wrongdoer or the wronged man: “it was not on account of the one who did wrong or the one who was harmed, but rather that your earnestness on our behalf would be made clear to you in the sight of God.” Titus came back refreshed and fonder of them than ever, remembering how they received him. Paul's boasting about them, made to Titus in advance, had proved true. The episode ends on the sentence the whole journey was traveling toward: “I rejoice that I can have complete confidence in you.”

title: Excel in This Grace of Giving
subtitle: 2 Corinthians 8:1–24
description: Macedonia's poverty overflowing into generosity, a gift measured by eagerness, and money handled so no one can criticize it.
paragraphs: Two whole chapters of this letter are given to a collection: money gathered from the Gentile churches for the poor saints in Jerusalem. Paul begins not with Corinth's duty but with somebody else's grace. “Now, brothers, we want you to know about the grace that God has given the churches of Macedonia.” The Macedonians were not rich churches funding a cause out of surplus. “In the terrible ordeal they suffered, their abundant joy and deep poverty overflowed into rich generosity.”

Paul testifies to the manner of it, because the manner is the sermon. “For I testify that they gave according to their ability and even beyond it. Of their own accord, they earnestly pleaded with us for the privilege of sharing in this service to the saints.” Nobody extracted it. They begged for the chance to give, and the deepest note in it comes last: “they gave themselves first to the Lord and then to us, through the will of God.”

Corinth had started earlier and stalled. Titus, who began the collection there, is being sent back to finish it: “So we urged Titus to help complete your act of grace, just as he had started it.” The appeal that follows flatters and challenges in the same sentence. The Corinthians excel in the visible gifts: “But just as you excel in everything,” in faith, speech, knowledge, earnestness, and love, “see that you also excel in this grace of giving.” And Paul is careful about the nature of the pressure. “I am not giving a command, but I am testing the sincerity of your love through the earnestness of others.”

The test is measured against Christ, not against Macedonia. “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though He was rich, yet for your sake He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich.” Then the practical counsel. They were first in desire last year, so the word is: “Now finish the work, so that you may complete it with the same eager desire, according to your means. For if the eagerness is there, the gift is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what he does not have.” The goal is not their burden. “It is not our intention that others may be relieved while you are burdened, but that there may be equality,” surplus meeting need in both directions in turn, under the old manna rule Paul quotes as the chapter's measuring line: “He who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall.”

The rest of the chapter is administration, and Paul treats administration as a holy thing. Titus comes eagerly, of his own will. A brother praised in all the churches travels with him, chosen by the churches to carry the gift. A third brother, proven earnest, joins them. The reasoning is stated without embarrassment: “We want to avoid any criticism of the way we administer this generous gift. For we are taking great care to do what is right, not only in the eyes of the Lord, but also in the eyes of men.” The chapter closes by commending the carriers and naming what the completed gift will prove: “In full view of the churches, then, show these men the proof of your love and the reason for our boasting about you.”

title: God Loves a Cheerful Giver
subtitle: 2 Corinthians 9:1–15
description: A promised gift prepared before it becomes a levy, seed and harvest, and a ministry that ends in thanksgiving.
paragraphs: The second collection chapter opens almost apologetically. “Now about the service to the saints, there is no need for me to write to you. For I know your eagerness to help, and I have been boasting to the Macedonians that since last year you in Achaia were prepared to give. And your zeal has stirred most of them to do likewise.” The two chapters lean on each other: Macedonia's giving provoked Corinth in the last one, and Corinth's zeal has provoked Macedonia in this one.

But the boasting creates a risk Paul names honestly. The brothers are being sent ahead “in order that our boasting about you in this matter should not prove empty, but that you will be prepared, just as I said.” If Macedonians arrive with him and find the gift unready, then “we,” and he adds the aside with the sting in it, “would be ashamed of having been so confident.” So the brothers go early, “to visit you beforehand and make arrangements for the generous gift you had promised. This way, your gift will be prepared generously and not begrudgingly.” A gift arranged in advance stays a gift. A gift scrambled for at the door becomes a levy.

Then the teaching on giving itself, set in farm language. “Remember this: Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows generously will also reap generously.” The amount, though, is left where Paul insists it belongs: “Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver.” No command, no quota, no compulsion. The heart decides, and God's love rests on the cheerfulness, not the size.

God's side of the exchange is ability, not pressure: “And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that in all things, at all times, having all that you need, you will abound in every good work.” The psalm line Paul quotes pictures God as the original scatterer of gifts: “He has scattered abroad His gifts to the poor; His righteousness endures forever.” The supply chain runs from God's hand: “Now He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your store of seed and will increase the harvest of your righteousness.” Enrichment, in this chapter, has a direction: “You will be enriched in every way to be generous on every occasion, and through us your generosity will produce thanksgiving to God.”

The end of the gift is not the money's arrival but what it produces at the other end. “For this ministry of service is not only supplying the needs of the saints but is also overflowing in many expressions of thanksgiving to God.” The saints who receive it “will glorify God for your obedient confession of the gospel of Christ,” and their prayers will run back toward the givers “because of the surpassing grace God has given you.” Then the whole two-chapter appeal bursts its banks in five words of a closing doxology: “Thanks be to God for His indescribable gift!”

title: Boast in the Lord
subtitle: 2 Corinthians 10:1–11:15
description: The letter turns: weapons that demolish strongholds, boasting kept inside the assigned field, and false apostles unmasked.
paragraphs: Here the letter turns. Nine chapters of comfort and explanation end, and what follows is defense, sharp enough that readers have felt the seam ever since. The telling walks the letter as it stands, one letter in the order Paul wrote it, and simply names the turn: from here to the end, Paul is fighting for this church against men who have come to Corinth in his absence and taught it to be ashamed of him.

He opens in Christ's own manner and signs it personally. “Now by the mildness and gentleness of Christ, I appeal to you,” I, Paul, the man the critics describe as humble in person and bold only at a distance. He begs them to make boldness unnecessary when he comes. The warfare he wages is real, but its weapons are not: “For though we live in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh. The weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the flesh. Instead, they have divine power to demolish strongholds. We demolish arguments and every presumption set up against the knowledge of God; and we take captive every thought to make it obedient to Christ.”

The Corinthians, he says, are judging by surfaces. “You are looking at outward appearances. If anyone is confident that he belongs to Christ, he should remind himself that we belong to Christ just as much as he does.” His authority, even boasted in, has a direction: “even if I boast somewhat excessively about the authority the Lord gave us for building you up rather than tearing you down, I will not be ashamed.”

Then the critics get quoted in their own words, the only sentence of theirs the letter preserves: “His letters are weighty and forceful, but his physical presence is unimpressive, and his speaking is of no account.” Paul's answer is a warning to take the letters at full value. “Such people should consider that what we are in our letters when absent, we will be in our actions when present.”

Against the new teachers' habit of grading themselves by themselves, he sets his own rule. “When they measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves with themselves, they show their ignorance.” His measure is assignment. “We, however, will not boast beyond our limits, but only within the field of influence that God has assigned to us,” a field that reaches Corinth itself, since “we were the first to reach you with the gospel of Christ.” The aim is outward, to regions beyond, not across the fence into another man's finished work. Then the rule that governs every boast in these chapters, quoted from Jeremiah: “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord.” “For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.”

The motive under the defense is a father's jealousy. “I am jealous for you with a godly jealousy. For I promised you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ. I am afraid, however, that just as Eve was deceived by the serpent’s cunning, your minds may be led astray from your simple and pure devotion to Christ.” What Corinth tolerates is the measure of the danger: “if someone comes and proclaims a Jesus other than the One we proclaimed, or if you receive a different spirit than the One you received, or a different gospel than the one you accepted, you put up with it very easily.”

Against the men he calls, with open irony, ‘super-apostles,’ Paul claims no inferiority, in knowledge whatever his speaking lacks. Then the old wound, reopened: he preached at Corinth free of charge. “Was it a sin for me to humble myself in order to exalt you, because I preached the gospel of God to you free of charge? I robbed other churches by accepting their support in order to serve you.” The refusal of their money was not a lack of love, and he will keep the policy, to cut the ground from the rivals who want to be counted his equals. Their true description comes last and unsparing: “For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, masquerading as apostles of Christ. And no wonder, for Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light.”

title: Boasting of Weakness
subtitle: 2 Corinthians 11:16–12:10
description: A fool's speech Paul apologizes for while giving it: a catalogue of scars, a basket over a wall, a thorn, and a refused prayer answered.
paragraphs: Paul now does the thing he has been refusing to do, and he labels it as he goes. “I repeat: Let no one take me for a fool. But if you do, then receive me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little.” The disclaimer is part of the performance: “In this confident boasting of mine, I am not speaking as the Lord would, but as a fool.” Since the church gladly endures fools who enslave and exploit it, it can endure this one. “Speaking as a fool, however, I can match what anyone else dares to boast about.”

The pedigree round is short, because on paper it is a draw. “Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they descendants of Abraham? So am I. Are they servants of Christ? (I am speaking as if I were out of my mind.) I am so much more.” Then the boast descends into the record no rival would claim as glory: “in harder labor, in more imprisonments, in worse beatings, in frequent danger of death.”

The numbers follow, flat as a charge sheet. “Five times I received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one. Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I was shipwrecked. I spent a night and a day in the open sea.” The dangers are listed by their addresses: rivers and bandits, countrymen and Gentiles, city and country, sea and false brothers, “in labor and toil and often without sleep, in hunger and thirst and often without food, in cold and exposure.” Above the whole list sits a pressure that never lifts: “Apart from these external trials, I face daily the pressure of my concern for all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is led into sin, and I do not burn with grief?”

The summation is the thesis of the whole speech. “If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.” And the story he chooses to prove it is an escape with nothing heroic in it. “The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, who is forever worthy of praise, knows that I am not lying. In Damascus, the governor under King Aretas secured the city of the Damascenes in order to arrest me. But I was lowered in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his grasp.” The apostle's great escape was a basket over a wall, carried by other people's hands.

Then the visions, and Paul's handling of them is as strange as the speech before them. “I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven. Whether it was in the body or out of it I do not know, but God knows.” The man is himself, held at arm's length in the third person. Of Paradise he reports only the limit: “The things he heard were inexpressible, things that man is not permitted to tell.” He will boast about that man, but not about himself, “except in my weaknesses,” and he refrains even from the truth of it, “so no one will credit me with more than he sees in me or hears from me.”

What followed the revelation is the episode's center. “So to keep me from becoming conceited, I was given a thorn in my flesh, a messenger of Satan, to torment me.” What the thorn was, the letter never says, and the telling does not guess. A person, a sickness, a recurring trouble: Paul leaves it unnamed, and it stays unnamed here. What he says is what he did with it. “Three times I pleaded with the Lord to take it away from me.”

The answer came instead of the removal, and it is quoted whole: “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.” Paul's response to a refused prayer becomes the conclusion of his boasting: “Therefore I will boast all the more gladly in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest on me. That is why, for the sake of Christ, I delight in weaknesses, in insults, in hardships, in persecutions, in difficulties. For when I am weak, then I am strong.”

title: Examine Yourselves
subtitle: 2 Corinthians 12:11–13:14
description: The defense closes with the test handed back to the testers, a third visit announced, and the blessing the church still repeats.
paragraphs: The boasting ends with the bill handed back to its cause. “I have become a fool, but you drove me to it. In fact, you should have commended me, since I am in no way inferior to those ‘super-apostles,’ even though I am nothing.” The evidence had been in front of them all along: “The marks of a true apostle,” “signs, wonders, and miracles,” “were performed among you with great perseverance.” The only respect in which Corinth was treated worse than other churches draws his driest apology: “In what way were you inferior to the other churches, except that I was not a burden to you? Forgive me this wrong!”

The third visit is announced as settled. “See, I am ready to come to you a third time, and I will not be a burden, because I am not seeking your possessions, but you.” Parents save for children, not children for parents: “And for the sake of your souls, I will most gladly spend my money and myself. If I love you more, will you love me less?” The last slander, that his refusal of their money was a trick to drain them through his messengers, gets two questions for an answer: “Did I exploit you by anyone I sent you? I urged Titus to visit you, and I sent our brother with him. Did Titus exploit you in any way? Did we not walk in the same Spirit and follow in the same footsteps?”

And the whole defense is re-labeled before it closes. “Have you been thinking all along that we were making a defense to you? We speak before God in Christ, and all of this, beloved, is to build you up.” Underneath it run his fears for the visit: quarreling and gossip and arrogance at Corinth, and grief for him “over many who have sinned earlier and have not repented of their acts of impurity, sexual immorality, and debauchery.”

The final chapter opens with the legal frame for a third coming. “This is the third time I am coming to you.” Then the rule of evidence, quoted from the law: “Every matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.” The warning given on the second visit is repeated from absence: “If I return, I will not spare anyone,” because they are demanding proof that Christ speaks through him, and the Christ who was “crucified in weakness, yet He lives by God’s power” is not weak in dealing with them.

Then the demand turns around. The Corinthians want Paul tested; Paul hands them the test. “Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; test yourselves. Do you not realize that Jesus Christ is in you,” unless the test is failed. His prayer for the outcome is the opposite of vindication: “Now we pray to God that you will not do anything wrong,” and, split by his own aside, “but that you will do what is right, even if we appear to have failed.” “For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth.” The reason for writing so severely from a distance is love of a practical kind: “This is why I write these things while absent, so that when I am present I will not need to be severe in my use of the authority that the Lord gave me for building you up, not for tearing you down.”

The letter that began with comfort ends with a benediction wide enough to hold everything it carried. “Finally, brothers, rejoice! Aim for perfect harmony, encourage one another, be of one mind, live in peace. And the God of love and peace will be with you. Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the saints send you greetings.” Then the words the church has repeated ever since, given here exactly as Paul gave them: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you.”
